message.content:
**Civil law**—the body of rules governing non‑criminal disputes between private individuals or entities—is built on several interlocking components. While specific terminology varies across jurisdictions, most systems share the following core elements: | Component | What it Covers | Typical Features | |-----------|-----------------|------------------| | **Sources of law** | Where the rules come from | • Statutory codes (e.g., contracts, torts, property)
• Case law / judicial precedent (especially in common‑law traditions)
• Regulations & administrative orders
• Customary practice (in some civil‑code states) | | **Substantive provisions** | Rights, duties, and responsibilities | • Contracts – formation, performance, breach, termination.
• Torts/Delicts – negligence, intentional wrongs, strict liability.
• Property – ownership, possession, transfer, easements.
• Family law – marriage, divorce, child custody, alimony.
• Succession/Wills – inheritance, intestate succession.
• Restitution & unjust enrichment – recovery when one party has been enriched at another’s expense without justification. | | **Procedural framework** | How claims are brought forward and adjudicated | • Jurisdictional requirements (personal, subject‑matter).
• Pleadings, discovery, pre‑trial motions.
• Trial conduct, evidence admissibility, burden of proof.
• Appeals process and appellate standards. | | **Remedies** | Ways courts can enforce or compensate | • Damages (compensatory, punitive, nominal).
• Specific performance (requiring fulfillment of contractual terms).
• Injunctions (preventative or mandatory actions).
• Declaratory judgments (clarification of legal status). | | **Legal doctrines & principles** | Underlying concepts guiding interpretation | • Good faith & fair dealing.
• Causation & proximate cause.
• Reliance & expectation interests.
• Res judicata & collateral estoppel.
• Doctrine of consideration (common‑law) or “good faith” (civil‑code). | | **Institutional actors** | Who applies and enforces the law | • Courts (judges, magistrates).
• Lawyers & counsel.
• Notaries (particularly in civil‑code countries).
• Administrative agencies (for regulatory compliance). | ### Key Takeaways 1. **Dual nature:** *Substantive* law defines what constitutes a claim (rights, duties); *procedural* law dictates how those claims are pursued and resolved. 2. **Variations by jurisdiction:** - In **common‑law** nations (U.S., U.K.), statutes codify many areas, but judicial decisions play a major role through stare decisis. - In **civil‑code** societies (France, Germany, Japan), comprehensive written codes dominate, though court interpretations still shape application. 3. **Interaction with other branches:** Civil law often intersects with constitutional limits (e.g., due process), commercial regulations, and international treaties affecting cross‑border transactions. Understanding these components provides a roadmap for navigating civil litigation—from drafting a contract to filing a lawsuit—and highlights why both statutory text and judicial reasoning matter equally in shaping outcomes.
